Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette: Robert Hayes was seventy-two hours into a double shift at his dental practice when his evening commute ended on the cold asphalt of a dimly lit parking garage. He had just secured the clinic doors, the familiar whir of the autoclave still echoing in his mind, when a marked cruiser blocked his vehicle. Before he could reach for his license, a heavy hand gripped the window frame, barking commands about his hands and his identity. The sudden escalation, the metallic clink of a holster, and the shouted orders that drowned out his own voice left him paralyzed. When they finally forced him to the ground, the concrete bruised his ribs and left a sharp, localized ache that now flared violently whenever he heard distant sirens. In the months that followed, Robert’s mind refused to let the incident settle. The memory felt like it belonged to someone else, a detached sequence of images, yet the auditory recall of the officers’ radios and the physical recall of the bruised ribs anchored it to his present body with terrifying clarity. Because he had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him that had invited that level of force, the memories grew sharper and more persistent, feeding directly into a deepening conviction that his life was irreparably destroyed and that the incident was a profound injustice that no authority had ever addressed. Conversely, each time those intrusive memories returned with their visceral urgency, they validated his sense of intrinsic fault and reinforced his belief that his life was completely ruined and the situation deeply unjust. The constant fear of strangers approaching him in ordinary settings soon dictated his daily routine. When a patient leaned too close during an exam, the memory of the arrest would flare, and the sudden pain recall would force him to abandon the appointment early, immediately driving him to avoid stressors and constantly scan the environment for signs of threat. When a patient leaned too close during an exam, the memory of the arrest would flare, making the present feel just as dangerous. This hypervigilance meant he rarely slept through the night; trouble falling or staying asleep kept him awake, and the resulting fatigue caused him to misinterpret ordinary neighborhood sounds as imminent danger, which would then directly trigger the auditory recall of the officers’ voices, pulling him back into the garage. In response to this escalating alarm, he began scanning every room before he entered it, always positioning himself in the dental chair closest to the exit. This safe seat seeking and his meticulous checking of the surroundings gradually bled into a broader refusal to engage with anything that might trigger stress or even unexpected positive emotions. Because he actively avoided stressors and avoided anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, his mind was denied the opportunity to process the event, and the memory of the encounter returned more frequently, feeling increasingly alien and physically painful. Simultaneously, his relentless avoidance made him feel entirely out of control of his own existence, which only reinforced his belief that there was something inherently flawed about him and that his life was completely ruined. As his threat monitoring intensified, causing him to perceive constant danger in his community, that sheer exhaustion of living in a state of perpetual alarm convinced him that the injustice was absolute and his life was truly destroyed. For years, Robert managed this cycle, but the weight of it finally fractured his professional life. During a routine crown preparation last Tuesday, a drill tip slipped, producing a high-pitched whine that matched the exact frequency of the police cruiser’s siren from that night. His hands froze, his vision tunneled, and he realized he could no longer look at his patients or sit at his own desk. He had come to believe that seeking help would force him to relive the garage, yet he sat in his therapist’s office now, terrified but certain that the only way to stop the pain was to finally face what he had spent years trying to outrun.
